**[I. Purpose and Scope]{.underline}**

This memorandum summarizes the rationale behind the dispute resolution provisions drafted by Harmon & Grey LLP across the three principal transaction documents comprising the Greenleaf Nutritionals / Pacifica Botanics strategic supply relationship: (i) the Exclusive Supply Agreement (the \"**SA**\"), (ii) the Quality Assurance Side Letter (the \"**QA Letter**\"), and (iii) the IP License Agreement (the \"**IPLA**\"), each to be entered into between Pacifica Botanics Pte. Ltd. (\"**Pacifica**\") and Greenleaf Nutritionals, Inc. (\"**Greenleaf**\").

Harmon & Grey drafted the initial arbitration and dispute resolution clauses across all three documents at Pacifica\'s instruction. This memorandum is being shared with Greenleaf\'s counsel, Whitfield & Crane LLP, to facilitate their review and to expedite negotiation of any proposed revisions in advance of the anticipated signing date of **July 18, 2025**, and the Target Effective Date of **August 1, 2025**. We respectfully request that Whitfield & Crane provide any comments on the dispute resolution provisions no later than July 11, 2025, to allow sufficient time for resolution before signing.

By way of commercial context, the transaction establishes a seven-year exclusive supply relationship with minimum annual purchase commitments of USD \$22,000,000 during Years 1 through 3 and USD \$28,000,000 during Years 4 through 7, for aggregate minimum commitments of approximately USD \$178,000,000 over the initial term. The SA further provides for two automatic three-year renewal periods, subject to certain conditions. Given the scale and duration of this relationship, the dispute resolution architecture was crafted with particular care to ensure that any disagreements between the parties are resolved efficiently, predictably, and with access to decision-makers possessing the appropriate institutional and subject-matter expertise.

**[II. Overview of the Dispute Resolution Framework]{.underline}**

The transaction documents employ a three-tier dispute resolution structure, with each agreement directing disputes to the institution and forum best suited to its subject matter. This architecture was designed deliberately to match the nature of the obligations under each agreement with the institutional competence and procedural tools most likely to produce efficient and well-reasoned outcomes.

**A. Supply Agreement --- Article 14 (ICC Arbitration)**

The SA, which constitutes the core commercial framework governing pricing, delivery schedules, exclusivity obligations, and termination rights, provides for arbitration under the Rules of Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce (\"**ICC**\"). The ICC\'s established reputation for administering complex international commercial disputes, its experienced Secretariat, and its global reach make it the natural institution for the principal commercial agreement in this transaction.

Pursuant to SA Section 14.1, any dispute arising out of or relating to the SA shall be finally resolved by arbitration administered by the ICC. The juridical seat of arbitration is Singapore (Section 14.2), selected because Pacifica is incorporated in Singapore and the curial law of Singapore provides a well-developed, pro-arbitration framework for international arbitration. The venue of hearings shall be London, England, given its position as a leading centre for international arbitration and its geographic midpoint between the parties\' principal operations. London was chosen as a neutral, convenient hearing location offering world-class arbitration facilities and infrastructure, and the distinction between the seat and the hearing location is a routine feature of modern international arbitration practice.

Section 14.3 provides that the arbitration shall be conducted by a sole arbitrator, with either party retaining the right to request a panel of three arbitrators within fifteen (15) days of service of the Request for Arbitration. This approach offers the parties flexibility, allowing straightforward disputes to proceed efficiently before a sole arbitrator while preserving the option for a full panel in matters of greater complexity or value.

The governing law of the SA is the law of the State of New York, United States, without regard to conflict-of-laws principles (Section 14.4). This reflects the fact that Greenleaf\'s commercial operations are centered in the United States and New York law is widely understood and applied in international commercial disputes of this nature.

**B. Quality Assurance Side Letter --- Section 7 (SIAC Expert Determination / Arbitration)**

The QA Letter, which governs product specifications, testing methodologies, acceptance criteria, and rejection rights, employs a specialized two-step dispute resolution mechanism under the auspices of the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (\"**SIAC**\").

In the first instance, technical quality disputes --- including disagreements regarding testing methodology, conformance to product specifications, and the exercise of rejection rights --- are submitted to expert determination under the SIAC Rules for the Appointment of Experts (Section 7.1). This mechanism was designed to ensure that disputes of a predominantly technical or scientific character are resolved by individuals with the relevant subject-matter expertise, rather than by generalist arbitrators. Expert determination offers a streamlined, cost-effective resolution pathway appropriate for the majority of quality-related disagreements likely to arise in the ordinary course of performance.

Where a dispute exceeds USD \$5,000,000 in value or where the expert determination is challenged, the matter escalates to full arbitration administered by SIAC (Section 7.2). The USD \$5,000,000 threshold was calibrated to distinguish routine quality disagreements --- which should be resolved quickly and inexpensively --- from material disputes warranting the procedural protections and comprehensive adjudication of a full arbitral proceeding.

SIAC was chosen as the administering institution for the QA Letter given its expertise in Asia-Pacific commercial disputes and the fact that its dedicated expert determination rules are well-suited to the technical quality issues likely to arise in connection with Pacifica\'s Singapore-based manufacturing and quality control operations.

The governing law of the QA Letter is Singapore law (Section 7.3), selected because the QA Letter primarily concerns Pacifica\'s manufacturing and testing operations conducted in Singapore, and Singapore law provides the most natural legal framework for interpreting obligations performed within the jurisdiction.

**C. IP License Agreement --- Section 9 (LCIA Arbitration)**

The IPLA, which governs the cross-licensing of certain intellectual property rights, regulatory data packages, and proprietary formulations, provides for arbitration under the Rules of the London Court of International Arbitration (\"**LCIA**\"). The LCIA was selected because the IPLA concerns intellectual property rights and regulatory data, which the parties considered best suited to London-seated arbitration under English law.

English law governs the IPLA (Section 9.2), reflecting the well-developed framework for IP licensing under English law and its widespread use in international intellectual property transactions. The arbitration shall be conducted by a sole arbitrator, in the English language.

Section 9.3 contains a consolidation provision intended as a practical efficiency measure to avoid duplicative proceedings. Where claims under the IPLA also relate to obligations arising under the SA, such claims shall be heard jointly in a single arbitration proceeding conducted under IPLA Section 9 and administered by the LCIA. This ensures that overlapping disputes touching both IP rights and supply obligations are resolved in a unified proceeding, avoiding the risk of inconsistent decisions and unnecessary costs.

**[III. Detailed Rationale for Key Provisions in Article 14 of the Supply Agreement]{.underline}**

**A. Seat and Venue Selection (Section 14.2)**

Singapore was selected as the juridical seat of arbitration under the SA for several compelling reasons. First, Singapore is a signatory to the 1958 New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, ensuring that any award rendered in a Singapore-seated arbitration is enforceable in over 170 contracting states, including the United States. Second, Singapore\'s International Arbitration Act (Cap. 143A), which incorporates the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration, provides a modern, pro-arbitration curial framework that is internationally recognized and trusted. Third, Pacifica is domiciled in Singapore, and situating the juridical seat in Singapore facilitates enforcement of any award against Pacifica\'s assets if necessary, thereby providing Greenleaf with meaningful recourse. Fourth, Singapore\'s courts have a strong and well-documented track record of minimal intervention in arbitral proceedings, consistent with international best practice.

London was selected as the physical hearing location on practical grounds. London is approximately equidistant between Charlotte, North Carolina --- where Greenleaf\'s principal offices are located --- and Singapore, providing a geographically convenient meeting point. London also offers world-class arbitration hearing facilities at institutions including the International Dispute Resolution Centre, and the availability of experienced international arbitrators based in or regularly traveling through London is a significant practical advantage. Additionally, both parties\' counsel maintain London-based resources and personnel, reducing logistical friction.

The distinction between the juridical seat and the physical venue of hearings is well-established in international arbitration practice and should not give rise to any procedural difficulty. The seat determines the curial law and the supervisory jurisdiction for any post-award challenge, while the hearing location is simply the place where oral hearings are convened as a matter of practical convenience. This arrangement is commonplace in major international arbitrations.

**B. Finality and Limited Appeal Right (Section 14.6)**

Section 14.6 was drafted to ensure the finality of arbitral awards while preserving a carefully defined \"safety valve\" allowing appeal on questions of law. This provision was modeled on the approach under the English Arbitration Act 1996, specifically Section 69, which permits parties to agree to appeal arbitral awards on questions of law to the courts. We believe this provision strikes an appropriate balance between finality and the ability to correct material errors of law. The availability of appellate review on points of law provides both parties with assurance that the tribunal\'s legal reasoning will be subject to judicial oversight, thereby enhancing the legitimacy and reliability of the arbitral process.

Section 14.6 provides that any appeal on a question of law arising out of an award shall be brought before the High Court of Singapore, sitting in its capacity as the supervisory court at the juridical seat. This channels post-award review to a single, predictable forum, avoiding the prospect of parallel or competing challenge proceedings in multiple jurisdictions.

Pacifica\'s recent experience with post-award challenges underscores the importance of this provision. In 2023, Pacifica prevailed in an ICC arbitration seated in Hong Kong against a Korean buyer, involving claims valued at approximately USD \$8,200,000 relating to rejected shipments. Following the award, the losing party challenged enforcement in Korean courts, citing alleged defects in the arbitration clause. Although the challenge was ultimately unsuccessful, it delayed enforcement by approximately fourteen months, imposing significant cost and commercial disruption on Pacifica. The appeal mechanism in Section 14.6 was drafted with the benefit of that experience, and is intended to ensure that any post-award review is channeled through a single, clearly defined appellate procedure before the courts at the seat, rather than arising unpredictably during enforcement proceedings abroad.

**C. Discovery Limitations (Section 14.5)**

Section 14.5 provides that no pre-hearing discovery, disclosure, or document production of any kind shall be ordered by the tribunal or requested by the parties. This provision was drafted deliberately and reflects Pacifica\'s strongly held view --- shared, we understand, by Greenleaf --- that international commercial arbitration is not intended to replicate the broad discovery mechanisms available in U.S. federal or state courts.

The international consensus, reflected in instruments such as the IBA Rules on the Taking of Evidence in International Arbitration, is that document production in international arbitration should be limited and targeted, rather than open-ended. Section 14.5 is consistent with this prevailing international norm and ensures that the arbitration proceeds on the basis of documentary evidence and witness testimony presented by the parties, without the burden, expense, and delay associated with extensive pre-hearing discovery.

The provision also serves an important commercial purpose. Pacifica\'s proprietary manufacturing processes, botanical extraction methodologies, and trade secrets are the cornerstone of its competitive position. Broad, U.S.-style discovery would expose Pacifica to the risk of fishing expeditions targeting these proprietary assets, with no guarantee that confidentiality orders would be sufficient to prevent disclosure to competitors. Section 14.5 eliminates this risk at the outset.

Critically, each party retains the right to present documentary evidence and witness testimony at the hearing. The restriction applies solely to compelled pre-hearing production; voluntary disclosure and submission of documentary evidence in support of a party\'s case are unaffected. This ensures that due process is preserved while eliminating the procedural burden that broad discovery would impose.

**D. Damages Limitations (Section 14.11)**

Section 14.11 contains a mutual waiver of punitive, exemplary, and consequential damages. This exclusion is standard in international supply agreements of this nature and ensures that the arbitral tribunal focuses on compensating actual, demonstrated losses rather than speculative or indirect harm. Both parties benefit from certainty as to the scope of potential liability, and the mutual character of the waiver ensures that neither party bears disproportionate exposure.

**E. Limitation Period (Section 14.9)**

Section 14.9 establishes a one-year limitation period for the commencement of arbitral proceedings. Given the nature of the supply relationship --- involving recurring shipments, ongoing quality monitoring, and annual pricing adjustments --- a one-year limitation period ensures that disputes are raised and resolved promptly, preventing the accumulation of stale claims that would be difficult to adjudicate fairly.

**F. Interim Relief (Section 14.7)**

Section 14.7 preserves each party\'s right to seek injunctive or other equitable relief from any court of competent jurisdiction, notwithstanding the arbitration agreement. This carve-out is standard and necessary to ensure that parties can protect their rights in urgent circumstances --- for example, misuse of licensed intellectual property or a supply disruption threatening public health or regulatory compliance.

**G. Cost Allocation (Section 14.8)**

Section 14.8 provides that the costs of arbitration, including reasonable legal fees, shall be borne by the unsuccessful party. This loser-pays fee-shifting mechanism is intended to discourage frivolous claims and encourage settlement.

**H. Confidentiality (Section 14.10)**

Section 14.10 requires that all arbitral proceedings, submissions, evidence, and awards remain confidential, subject to a limited carve-out for disclosures required by applicable law or regulation. This provision is standard and protects both parties\' proprietary and commercially sensitive information.

**[IV. Cross-Agreement Coordination]{.underline}**

The three transaction documents each contain bespoke dispute resolution provisions tailored to the subject matter of the respective agreement. This approach reflects the distinct character of the obligations in each instrument: the SA\'s commercial and supply terms, the QA Letter\'s technical quality requirements, and the IPLA\'s intellectual property and regulatory data provisions.

The parties have addressed the potential for overlap or inconsistency through the integration and merger clause in SA Section 15.8, which establishes a clear hierarchy among the transaction documents. In the event of any conflict between the terms of the SA and the terms of the QA Letter or IPLA, the SA shall control. This integration clause provides a clear and enforceable hierarchy, ensuring that the SA\'s terms take precedence in the event of any ambiguity or inconsistency across the document suite.

We recognize that the parties may wish to discuss whether to harmonize certain procedural aspects of the dispute resolution mechanisms --- for example, aligning timelines for notice or agreeing on common procedural calendars where disputes under multiple agreements arise concurrently. We are open to such discussions. However, we are of the view that the current structure, which reflects commercial and legal realities specific to each agreement, is workable and does not require fundamental restructuring. The distinct institutions and governing laws selected for each agreement ensure that each type of dispute is resolved by the decision-maker and under the legal framework best suited to the issues at hand.

**[V. Pacifica\'s Arbitration Experience and Lessons Learned]{.underline}**

As noted above, Pacifica\'s 2023 ICC arbitration provides important context for the current dispute resolution architecture. In that matter, Pacifica brought claims valued at approximately USD \$8,200,000 against a Korean buyer arising from the wrongful rejection of multiple shipments of botanical extract. The arbitration was seated in Hong Kong and conducted under ICC Rules. Pacifica obtained a favorable award.

However, the losing party challenged enforcement in the Korean courts, contending that the arbitration clause was \"pathological\" due to certain alleged ambiguities in the clause\'s drafting. Although the Korean court ultimately rejected the challenge and permitted enforcement, the proceedings delayed recovery by approximately fourteen months and imposed substantial additional legal costs on Pacifica.

The arbitration provisions in the current transaction documents were drafted with the benefit of that experience. Our objective was to minimize the risk of post-award challenge and enforcement delay by ensuring that each arbitration clause is clear, specific, and enforceable, with well-defined institutional rules, seat designations, and procedural parameters. We are confident that the current provisions achieve this objective.

**[VI. Conclusion and Recommendation]{.underline}**

Harmon & Grey is confident that the dispute resolution framework across the SA, QA Letter, and IPLA is comprehensive, balanced, and enforceable. The three-tier structure matches each agreement\'s subject matter with the institution, governing law, and procedural mechanism best suited to resolve disputes efficiently and predictably.

We recommend that Pacifica share this memorandum with Greenleaf\'s counsel at Whitfield & Crane LLP to facilitate efficient negotiation of any proposed revisions to the dispute resolution provisions. Harmon & Grey remains available to discuss any questions from Pacifica\'s management team or from Greenleaf\'s counsel. We are willing to consider reasonable adjustments to the current provisions, while noting that the core architecture reflects Pacifica\'s strong preference for Singapore-connected dispute resolution and was carefully designed in light of Pacifica\'s prior arbitration experience.

The new encapsulation co-manufacturer (expected Q1 2026) makes this worse unless it is addressed now.",
    "**SA s.14.6 appeal on questions of law to the High Court of Singapore** (Issue 5). It conflicts with the \"final and binding\" language, with ICC Rules Art. 35(6), and (on our understanding, to be confirmed by Singapore counsel) with the Singapore International Arbitration Act, which does not provide for appeals on points of law. This is the clearest \"pathological\" feature in the package.",

para("The package also leans in Pacifica's favor procedurally. Pacifica's most likely claims are debt claims: unpaid invoices, the 15% Shortfall Fee (SA s.4.2) and the 25% convenience-termination fee (SA s.13.4). They are documentary, they are carved out of the liability cap (SA s.11.1(d)), and they do not depend on discovery, consequential loss or a long limitation period. Greenleaf's most likely claims are the reverse. They are quality, contamination and recall claims, which depend on Pacifica's own batch records and test data, surface late (latent defects), and produce mostly what New York law calls consequential loss. Article 14 cuts off exactly those three things: discovery (s.14.5), time (s.14.9) and consequential damages (s.14.11).")
para("We identify **26 issues**: **7 Critical**, **8 High**, **8 Medium** and **3 Low**. The Critical items, which must be fixed before signing, are:")
for x in [
    "**Fragmented, uncoordinated architecture** (Issues 1-2). The three documents cover overlapping subject matter in a single transaction but send disputes to three institutions under three laws. They have no cross-document consolidation mechanism, and their precedence clauses go in circles. One defective batch could produce an ICC arbitration, a SIAC expert determination, a SIAC arbitration and a fight over which of them has jurisdiction.",
    "**IPLA s.9.3** (Issue 3). It requires IPLA claims that \"also relate to\" Supply Agreement obligations to be heard in a single **LCIA** arbitration. That directly contradicts the ICC clause in SA s.14.1. In its July 3 memo, Harmon & Grey confirms the intent is to pull related SA disputes into the LCIA.",
    "**No joinder or third-party mechanism** (Issue 4). Greenleaf's co-manufacturers are bound by purchase orders with NC law and NC state-court forum clauses, so Greenleaf would arbitrate against Pacifica abroad while litigating against the co-manufacturer in Mecklenburg County. The new encapsulation co-manufacturer (expected Q1 2026) makes this worse unless it is addressed now.",
    "**SA s.14.6 appeal on questions of law to the High Court of Singapore** (Issue 5). It conflicts with the \"final and binding\" language, with ICC Rules Art. 35(6), and (on our understanding, to be confirmed by Singapore counsel) with the Singapore International Arbitration Act, which does not provide for appeals on points of law. This is the clearest \"pathological\" feature in the package.",
    "**SA s.14.11 consequential damages bar** (Issue 6). It is framed as a limit on the tribunal's **authority** rather than as a substantive waiver, which turns any damages dispute into a potential excess-of-mandate challenge. It has none of the carve-outs found in SA s.11.2, and it conflicts with QA s.6.6 and s.7.2. Greenleaf's management has said it would walk away rather than accept a blanket consequential damages waiver on this deal. We agree this is a Tier 1 point.",
]:
    bullet(x)
para("The High items are the discovery bar (s.14.5), the one-year limitation period (s.14.9), the QA Side Letter's expert-determination mechanics and its reference to SIAC rules we could not verify, the illusory finality of expert determination and the undefined US$5 million escalation threshold, the Singapore-law/New York-law split (which gives \"consequential\" two different meanings in the same deal), the unfinalized Specifications that any expert would have to apply, and the enforcement/set-off position.")
para("**Recommended approach.** Replace the three clauses with a **single, identical dispute resolution clause** in all three Transaction Documents, or a short stand-alone Dispute Resolution Agreement incorporated into each. It should have one institution (ICC, which is Pacifica's own choice for the principal agreement), one seat, one governing law (New York), an express multi-contract, consolidation and joinder consent, an optional technical expert stage that cannot bar or delay arbitration, tribunal-managed document production under the IBA Rules, and no appeal on points of law. Remedy limitations should sit in the substantive liability article, with carve-outs that protect Greenleaf's recall, cover and lost-profit exposure. Because Mr. Heller and Mr. Park have both said Singapore is not a dealbreaker, **accepting Singapore as the seat is our principal trade**. Section VII sets out a full draft clause. Section VIII sets out the negotiating sequence.")
para("**Answers to the specific questions in the June 30-July 1 email chain:**")
for x in [
    "**Does the QA Side Letter's expert determination help with the co-manufacturer problem?** No. As drafted it makes the problem worse. It adds another forum, it binds only Greenleaf and Pacifica, and either party can bypass it by \"challenging\" the determination (Issues 17-18). A restructured, optional technical-expert stage could help, because it can produce a neutral finding on whether the extract was in specification. That finding is useful in any later proceeding with a co-manufacturer (Section VII).",
    "**Is the one-year limitation period (s.14.9) enforceable under New York law?** Probably yes, so Greenleaf should not count on a court striking it down. New York lets parties shorten limitation periods by written agreement if the shorter period is reasonable (CPLR 201). For sales of goods, N.Y. U.C.C. § 2-725(1) allows the period to be reduced to as little as one year. The clause has to be fixed by negotiation (Issue 8).",
    "**Does a Singapore seat create U.S. enforcement wrinkles?** Not in itself. Singapore and the United States are both New York Convention states, and a Singapore award is enforceable in North Carolina or Delaware under Chapter 2 of the FAA (9 U.S.C. §§ 201-208). The real enforcement risks come from the clauses themselves (Issues 3, 5, 6, 7 and 9). In practice, an award in Greenleaf's favor will most likely be enforced against Pacifica's assets **in Singapore**, where a Singapore-seated award is enforced as a domestic award (Issue 24).",
]:
    bullet(x)

h("V. Detailed Analysis", 1)
h("A. Cross-Document Architecture", 2)

issue("1", "Three institutions, three governing laws, no coordination", "Critical",
 "SA ss.14.1, 14.2, 14.4, 15.11; QA ss.7.1-7.3; IPLA ss.9.1-9.2",
 "SA: ICC, seat Singapore, hearings London, NY law. QA: SIAC expert determination, then SIAC arbitration, seat Singapore, Singapore law. IPLA: LCIA, seat London, English law, sole arbitrator.",
 ["The three documents are expressly one integrated transaction. The SA recitals say the QA Letter and IPLA \"form part of the transaction contemplated by this Agreement\". SA s.3.3 and s.8.2 incorporate them by reference. QA s.8.1 says the QA Letter \"supplements and forms part of the Supply Agreement\". IPLA s.2.1 says the license consideration \"flows through the minimum purchase commitments\" of the SA. Yet each document sends disputes to a different institution, under a different law, with different procedural rules. Harmon & Grey calls this a deliberate \"three-tier\" design. In practice the tiers overlap on almost every realistic dispute:",
  "**A contaminated curcumin batch** is at once (i) a Nonconformity and rejection dispute under QA ss.3.4/5.4, which goes to SIAC expert determination; (ii) a recall cost dispute under QA s.6, which goes to SIAC expert determination and then SIAC arbitration; (iii) a breach of the SA s.9.2 warranties and an SA s.10.1 indemnity claim, which goes to ICC; and (iv) if Greenleaf relied on Pacifica's Licensed IP data in an FDA filing that is now inaccurate, an IPLA s.3.3/7.2(c) claim, which goes to LCIA (or, through IPLA s.9.3, an LCIA proceeding that also absorbs the SA claims).",
  "**Consolidation across institutions is not available.** ICC Rules Art. 10 consolidates only ICC arbitrations. LCIA Rules (2020) Arts. 22.1(ix)-(x) and 22A apply only to LCIA arbitrations under the same or compatible agreements. The SIAC Rules likewise apply only within SIAC. No tribunal can order an ICC, SIAC and LCIA proceeding to be heard together without fresh consent from both parties, which a respondent rarely gives once a dispute has arisen.",
  "**Inconsistent outcomes are a real risk.** An SIAC expert could find a batch in specification while an ICC tribunal finds the same batch defective under the SA definition (which differs: Issue 21). Each tribunal is applying different law (Issue 20) and different remedy rules (Issue 6).",
  "**Jurisdictional skirmishing comes first.** Each respondent will be able to argue that the claim belongs before a different body. Pacifica's own 2023 experience shows that challenges grounded in clause ambiguity can delay recovery by more than a year."],
 "Greenleaf's most likely dispute, a quality failure that leads to a recall (Mr. Heller's email of June 30), is exactly the dispute that falls between all three documents. Fragmentation multiplies cost and gives the better-resourced or better-positioned party leverage to choose its forum. It also makes it hard to obtain one enforceable award covering all of Greenleaf's loss. Mr. Park's concern about \"parallel proceedings, inconsistent results, and a lot of wasted legal spend\" is well-founded.",
 ["Replace SA Art. 14, QA s.7 and IPLA s.9 with **one identical dispute resolution clause** (or a stand-alone Dispute Resolution Agreement incorporated by reference into each) covering any dispute \"arising out of or in connection with any Transaction Document\" (draft in Section VII).",
  "**One institution: ICC.** It is Pacifica's own choice for the principal agreement, and it has well-developed multi-contract (Art. 9), joinder (Art. 7) and consolidation (Art. 10) provisions. The ICC Secretariat also has a case-management office in Singapore, which meets Pacifica's stated preference for Singapore-connected dispute resolution.",
  "**One seat and one governing law.** Our preference is New York law for all three documents (Issue 20), with the seat as the principal trade (Issue 9 / Section VIII).",
  "Add an express statement that the arbitration agreements in the Transaction Documents are **compatible** and that claims under more than one Transaction Document may be brought in a single arbitration (ICC Art. 9) or consolidated (ICC Art. 10)."],
 "If Pacifica insists on keeping separate clauses, require at a minimum (i) the same institution and seat in all three, (ii) an express consent to consolidation and to a single tribunal for related disputes, and (iii) a rule that the first-constituted tribunal decides any overlap question with binding effect.")

issue("2", "Circular precedence clauses", "Critical",
 "SA ss.3.3, 15.8; QA s.8.1; IPLA s.10.3",
 "SA s.15.8: \"In the event of a conflict between the terms of this Agreement and the terms of the QA Side Letter or the IPLA, this Agreement shall control.\" QA s.8.1: the Supply Agreement controls, \"provided, however, that with respect to the subject matters specifically addressed in this Side Letter - including ... the dispute resolution mechanism set forth in Section 7 - this Side Letter shall control.\" IPLA s.10.3: the Supply Agreement controls \"except with respect to matters specifically and exclusively addressed by this Agreement.\"",
 ["Harmon & Grey's memo (s.IV) says SA s.15.8 \"establishes a clear hierarchy\" ensuring \"the SA's terms take precedence.\" It does not. The three clauses point in different directions:",
  "SA s.15.8 says the SA always controls. QA s.8.1 says the QA Letter controls on dispute resolution. The two are irreconcilable for a quality dispute that falls within both SA s.14.1 (\"any dispute ... relating to this Agreement\") and QA s.7.1 (\"exclusively by expert determination\").",
  "SA s.3.3 says that on conflicts over \"quality standards, testing protocols, or related matters\" the SA controls \"subject to Section 15.8\". That is circular, because s.15.8 is the same rule.",
  "IPLA s.10.3 makes the SA control except for matters \"specifically and exclusively addressed\" by the IPLA. Pacifica will say dispute resolution for IPLA claims, including the s.9.3 joint-hearing rule, is \"specifically and exclusively addressed\" by the IPLA.",
  "Each document is signed at the same time and \"supplements\" the others. A tribunal could equally apply the later-in-time, the more specific, or the governing-document rule. The answer will probably differ depending on which tribunal is asked first."],
 "This is the clause on which any jurisdictional objection will turn. A Greenleaf ICC claim for defective product could face an objection that it belongs exclusively to SIAC expert determination. A Greenleaf SIAC claim could face the objection that SA s.15.8 sends it to the ICC. Either objection, if it fails, can be re-run at the set-aside stage (UNCITRAL Model Law Art. 34(2)(a)(iii)) or at enforcement (New York Convention Art. V(1)(c)). That is the \"pathological clause\" risk the client wants eliminated.",
 ["Adopt a single express hierarchy in all three documents. The unified dispute resolution clause governs every dispute under any Transaction Document and prevails over any inconsistent provision in any of them. Delete QA s.8.1's dispute resolution proviso and IPLA s.9.3, and conform IPLA s.10.3.",
  "Delete the circular words \"subject to Section 15.8\" from SA s.3.3, and state expressly which document controls each substantive topic (e.g., the QA Letter controls testing protocols and the rejection/recall mechanics; the SA controls price, volume, exclusivity and liability)."])

issue("3", "IPLA s.9.3 pulls Supply Agreement disputes into the LCIA", "Critical",
 "IPLA s.9.3 (with IPLA s.10.3; SA ss.14.1, 15.8)",
 "\"For the avoidance of doubt, claims arising under this Agreement that also relate to obligations under the Supply Agreement shall be heard jointly in a single arbitration proceeding under this Section 9.\"",
 ["Section 9.3 is labelled a consolidation clause. In effect it moves disputes from one forum to another. Harmon & Grey's memo (s.II.C) confirms that the intended result is a \"single arbitration proceeding conducted under IPLA Section 9 and administered by the LCIA\". Read with SA s.14.1, it creates a direct conflict:",
  "Almost every IPLA claim \"relates to\" SA obligations. The license is granted for products \"supplied under the Supply Agreement\" (definition of Authorized Purpose). Its consideration is the SA minimum purchase commitment (IPLA s.2.1). It ends automatically when the SA ends (IPLA s.6.3). Section 2.2(d) prohibits using the Licensed IP to source from other suppliers, which overlaps the SA exclusivity provisions.",
  "Section 9.3 gives Pacifica the option, by starting with an IPLA claim, to pull SA claims (the Shortfall Fee, the termination fee, exclusivity) into a London-seated LCIA arbitration under English law before a sole arbitrator. That is the opposite of what SA s.14.1 provides, and it would allow forum selection after a dispute has arisen.",
  "Conversely, Greenleaf could face competing ICC and LCIA proceedings on the same facts. Each tribunal would decide its own jurisdiction (competence-competence), and the parties could end up seeking anti-suit or anti-arbitration relief. Because the IPLA is seated in London and the SA in Singapore, supervisory jurisdiction is split between the English and Singapore courts.",
  "The clause also does not say which law, which costs rule (IPLA s.9.4 each party bears its own costs; SA s.14.8 loser pays) or which damages rule applies to the SA claims once they are inside the LCIA proceeding."],
 "This is the most serious drafting risk in the package. It is a clause that Pacifica can use tactically and that undermines SA Article 14 entirely. It also contradicts Harmon & Grey's own stated aim of clear, single-forum post-award review.",
 ["Delete IPLA s.9.3.",
  "Replace it with the unified clause's multi-contract and consolidation consent, so that related IPLA and SA claims are heard together **in one ICC arbitration** under the same rules, seat and law."],
 "If Pacifica insists on keeping the LCIA for pure IP-misuse claims (an outcome we do not recommend), s.9.3 must be reversed so that IPLA claims connected with the SA are heard in the ICC arbitration under SA Art. 14. The IPLA should not be able to absorb SA claims.")

issue("4", "No joinder, consolidation or third-party mechanism (co-manufacturers; Ridgeway)", "Critical",
 "SA Art. 14; QA s.7; IPLA s.9; Greenleaf co-manufacturer purchase orders (not reviewed)",
 "None of the three clauses contains any consent to joinder of additional parties, intervention or consolidation with proceedings involving third parties. SA s.15.9 and IPLA s.10.8 exclude third-party beneficiaries.",
 ["Greenleaf's model depends on U.S. co-manufacturers for blending, encapsulation and packaging. The email chain notes that the existing co-manufacturer arrangements use purchase orders with North Carolina choice of law and forum selection for NC state courts, and that a new encapsulation co-manufacturer is expected to come online in Q1 2026.",
  "In a contamination scenario (Mr. Heller's example: a bad curcumin batch processed into 500,000 capsules), Greenleaf will need to blame Pacifica's extraction process and the co-manufacturer's incoming QC at the same time. Under the current documents it would arbitrate against Pacifica (ICC, Singapore seat, London hearings, or SIAC) while suing the co-manufacturer in Mecklenburg County Superior Court. Each respondent would argue the other caused the loss. Greenleaf could lose in both forums on inconsistent findings (\"empty chair\" risk).",
  "Under ICC Rules Art. 7, an additional party can be joined only if it is bound by an arbitration agreement, or (after the tribunal is constituted) if all parties, including the additional party, agree (Art. 7(5)). The co-manufacturers have no arbitration agreement with Pacifica and no incentive to consent. The QA expert determination binds only Greenleaf and Pacifica, so its findings would not bind a co-manufacturer.",
  "Ridgeway (about 62% equity holder; an \"Affiliate\" of Greenleaf under the IPLA definition) has no mechanism to participate. Mr. Park describes this as a secondary concern. We agree: Ridgeway's interests are better protected through confidentiality carve-outs (Issue 15) and governance arrangements with Greenleaf than through a right to intervene."],
 "This is client priority 2 and goes to the core of Greenleaf's most likely loss scenario. Parallel proceedings duplicate cost and evidence-gathering. They also expose Greenleaf to findings in one forum that defeat its claim in the other.",
 ["**Consent to joinder and consolidation.** Pacifica consents, in advance, to the joinder of any Affiliate of either party and of any \"Related Party\" (Greenleaf's co-manufacturers, contract packagers, contract laboratories and carriers) that agrees in writing to be bound. It also consents to consolidation of an arbitration under the Transaction Documents with any arbitration between Greenleaf and a Related Party under a compatible ICC clause, before a single tribunal.",
  "**Greenleaf litigation option for multi-party quality disputes.** Where a claim by Greenleaf against Pacifica arises from the same facts as a claim against a Related Party that is not bound to arbitrate, Greenleaf may elect (within 30 days of the Request for Arbitration or Answer) to have that dispute decided in the state or federal courts sitting in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina (or New York County, New York), and Pacifica submits to that jurisdiction and appoints a U.S. process agent. Singapore and New York courts generally uphold asymmetric option clauses between commercial parties (e.g., Dyna-Jet Pte Ltd v Wilson Taylor Asia Pacific Pte Ltd [2017] SGCA 32), but the clause must be drafted precisely.",
  "**Evidence-sharing covenant.** Pacifica agrees to provide documents, retained samples (QA s.2.3) and witness cooperation in any proceeding between Greenleaf and a Related Party concerning Products, subject to confidentiality protections.",
  "**Greenleaf internal action.** Going forward, including for the Q1 2026 encapsulation co-manufacturer, require co-manufacturing agreements to contain an ICC arbitration clause compatible with the unified clause (same rules, seat and language) and an express consent to joinder and consolidation with arbitrations under the Pacifica Transaction Documents. Consider amending existing co-manufacturer purchase orders on renewal."],
 "If Pacifica refuses the litigation option, insist on (i) the advance joinder/consolidation consent; (ii) a covenant that Pacifica will not object to the tribunal sitting on the same timetable as, or coordinating with, the related court proceeding; and (iii) Pacifica's agreement to be bound by findings of the technical expert (Section VII) that are also put before the court.")

h("V. Detailed Analysis", 1)
h("A. Cross-Document Architecture", 2)

issue("1", "Three institutions, three governing laws, no coordination", "Critical",
 "SA ss.14.1, 14.2, 14.4, 15.11; QA ss.7.1-7.3; IPLA ss.9.1-9.2",
 "SA: ICC, seat Singapore, hearings London, NY law. QA: SIAC expert determination, then SIAC arbitration, seat Singapore, Singapore law. IPLA: LCIA, seat London, English law, sole arbitrator.",
 ["The three documents are expressly one integrated transaction. The SA recitals say the QA Letter and IPLA \"form part of the transaction contemplated by this Agreement\". SA s.3.3 and s.8.2 incorporate them by reference. QA s.8.1 says the QA Letter \"supplements and forms part of the Supply Agreement\". IPLA s.2.1 says the license consideration \"flows through the minimum purchase commitments\" of the SA. Yet each document sends disputes to a different institution, under a different law, with different procedural rules. Harmon & Grey calls this a deliberate \"three-tier\" design. In practice the tiers overlap on almost every realistic dispute:",
  "**A contaminated curcumin batch** is at once (i) a Nonconformity and rejection dispute under QA ss.3.4/5.4, which goes to SIAC expert determination; (ii) a recall cost dispute under QA s.6, which goes to SIAC expert determination and then SIAC arbitration; (iii) a breach of the SA s.9.2 warranties and an SA s.10.1 indemnity claim, which goes to ICC; and (iv) if Greenleaf relied on Pacifica's Licensed IP data in an FDA filing that is now inaccurate, an IPLA s.3.3/7.2(c) claim, which goes to LCIA (or, through IPLA s.9.3, an LCIA proceeding that also absorbs the SA claims).",
  "**Consolidation across institutions is not available.** ICC Rules Art. 10 consolidates only ICC arbitrations. LCIA Rules (2020) Arts. 22.1(ix)-(x) and 22A apply only to LCIA arbitrations under the same or compatible agreements. The SIAC Rules likewise apply only within SIAC. No tribunal can order an ICC, SIAC and LCIA proceeding to be heard together without fresh consent from both parties, which a respondent rarely gives once a dispute has arisen.",
  "**Inconsistent outcomes are a real risk.** An SIAC expert could find a batch in specification while an ICC tribunal finds the same batch defective under the SA definition (which differs: Issue 21). Each tribunal is applying different law (Issue 20) and different remedy rules (Issue 6).",
  "**Jurisdictional skirmishing comes first.** Each respondent will be able to argue that the claim belongs before a different body. Pacifica's own 2023 experience shows that challenges grounded in clause ambiguity can delay recovery by more than a year."],
 "Greenleaf's most likely dispute, a quality failure that leads to a recall (Mr. Heller's email of June 30), is exactly the dispute that falls between all three documents. Fragmentation multiplies cost and gives the better-resourced or better-positioned party leverage to choose its forum. It also makes it hard to obtain one enforceable award covering all of Greenleaf's loss. Mr. Park's concern about \"parallel proceedings, inconsistent results, and a lot of wasted legal spend\" is well-founded.",
 ["Replace SA Art. 14, QA s.7 and IPLA s.9 with **one identical dispute resolution clause** (or a stand-alone Dispute Resolution Agreement incorporated by reference into each) covering any dispute \"arising out of or in connection with any Transaction Document\" (draft in Section VII).",
  "**One institution: ICC.** It is Pacifica's own choice for the principal agreement, and it has well-developed multi-contract (Art. 9), joinder (Art. 7) and consolidation (Art. 10) provisions. The ICC Secretariat also has a case-management office in Singapore, which meets Pacifica's stated preference for Singapore-connected dispute resolution.",
  "**One seat and one governing law.** Our preference is New York law for all three documents (Issue 20), with the seat as the principal trade (Issue 9 / Section VIII).",
  "Add an express statement that the arbitration agreements in the Transaction Documents are **compatible** and that claims under more than one Transaction Document may be brought in a single arbitration (ICC Art. 9) or consolidated (ICC Art. 10)."],
 "If Pacifica insists on keeping separate clauses, require at a minimum (i) the same institution and seat in all three, (ii) an express consent to consolidation and to a single tribunal for related disputes, and (iii) a rule that the first-constituted tribunal decides any overlap question with binding effect.")

issue("2", "Circular precedence clauses", "Critical",
 "SA ss.3.3, 15.8; QA s.8.1; IPLA s.10.3",
 "SA s.15.8: \"In the event of a conflict between the terms of this Agreement and the terms of the QA Side Letter or the IPLA, this Agreement shall control.\" QA s.8.1: the Supply Agreement controls, \"provided, however, that with respect to the subject matters specifically addressed in this Side Letter - including ... the dispute resolution mechanism set forth in Section 7 - this Side Letter shall control.\" IPLA s.10.3: the Supply Agreement controls \"except with respect to matters specifically and exclusively addressed by this Agreement.\"",
 ["Harmon & Grey's memo (s.IV) says SA s.15.8 \"establishes a clear hierarchy\" ensuring \"the SA's terms take precedence.\" It does not. The three clauses point in different directions:",
  "SA s.15.8 says the SA always controls. QA s.8.1 says the QA Letter controls on dispute resolution. The two are irreconcilable for a quality dispute that falls within both SA s.14.1 (\"any dispute ... relating to this Agreement\") and QA s.7.1 (\"exclusively by expert determination\").",
  "SA s.3.3 says that on conflicts over \"quality standards, testing protocols, or related matters\" the SA controls \"subject to Section 15.8\". That is circular, because s.15.8 is the same rule.",
  "IPLA s.10.3 makes the SA control except for matters \"specifically and exclusively addressed\" by the IPLA. Pacifica will say dispute resolution for IPLA claims, including the s.9.3 joint-hearing rule, is \"specifically and exclusively addressed\" by the IPLA.",
  "Each document is signed at the same time and \"supplements\" the others. A tribunal could equally apply the later-in-time, the more specific, or the governing-document rule. The answer will probably differ depending on which tribunal is asked first."],
 "This is the clause on which any jurisdictional objection will turn. A Greenleaf ICC claim for defective product could face an objection that it belongs exclusively to SIAC expert determination. A Greenleaf SIAC claim could face the objection that SA s.15.8 sends it to the ICC. Either objection, if it fails, can be re-run at the set-aside stage (UNCITRAL Model Law Art. 34(2)(a)(iii)) or at enforcement (New York Convention Art. V(1)(c)). That is the \"pathological clause\" risk the client wants eliminated.",
 ["Adopt a single express hierarchy in all three documents. The unified dispute resolution clause governs every dispute under any Transaction Document and prevails over any inconsistent provision in any of them. Delete QA s.8.1's dispute resolution proviso and IPLA s.9.3, and conform IPLA s.10.3.",
  "Delete the circular words \"subject to Section 15.8\" from SA s.3.3, and state expressly which document controls each substantive topic (e.g., the QA Letter controls testing protocols and the rejection/recall mechanics; the SA controls price, volume, exclusivity and liability)."])

issue("3", "IPLA s.9.3 pulls Supply Agreement disputes into the LCIA", "Critical",
 "IPLA s.9.3 (with IPLA s.10.3; SA ss.14.1, 15.8)",
 "\"For the avoidance of doubt, claims arising under this Agreement that also relate to obligations under the Supply Agreement shall be heard jointly in a single arbitration proceeding under this Section 9.\"",
 ["Section 9.3 is labelled a consolidation clause. In effect it moves disputes from one forum to another. Harmon & Grey's memo (s.II.C) confirms that the intended result is a \"single arbitration proceeding conducted under IPLA Section 9 and administered by the LCIA\". Read with SA s.14.1, it creates a direct conflict:",
  "Almost every IPLA claim \"relates to\" SA obligations. The license is granted for products \"supplied under the Supply Agreement\" (definition of Authorized Purpose). Its consideration is the SA minimum purchase commitment (IPLA s.2.1). It ends automatically when the SA ends (IPLA s.6.3). Section 2.2(d) prohibits using the Licensed IP to source from other suppliers, which overlaps the SA exclusivity provisions.",
  "Section 9.3 gives Pacifica the option, by starting with an IPLA claim, to pull SA claims (the Shortfall Fee, the termination fee, exclusivity) into a London-seated LCIA arbitration under English law before a sole arbitrator. That is the opposite of what SA s.14.1 provides, and it would allow forum selection after a dispute has arisen.",
  "Conversely, Greenleaf could face competing ICC and LCIA proceedings on the same facts. Each tribunal would decide its own jurisdiction (competence-competence), and the parties could end up seeking anti-suit or anti-arbitration relief. Because the IPLA is seated in London and the SA in Singapore, supervisory jurisdiction is split between the English and Singapore courts.",
  "The clause also does not say which law, which costs rule (IPLA s.9.4 each party bears its own costs; SA s.14.8 loser pays) or which damages rule applies to the SA claims once they are inside the LCIA proceeding."],
 "This is the most serious drafting risk in the package. It is a clause that Pacifica can use tactically and that undermines SA Article 14 entirely. It also contradicts Harmon & Grey's own stated aim of clear, single-forum post-award review.",
 ["Delete IPLA s.9.3.",
  "Replace it with the unified clause's multi-contract and consolidation consent, so that related IPLA and SA claims are heard together **in one ICC arbitration** under the same rules, seat and law."],
 "If Pacifica insists on keeping the LCIA for pure IP-misuse claims (an outcome we do not recommend), s.9.3 must be reversed so that IPLA claims connected with the SA are heard in the ICC arbitration under SA Art. 14. The IPLA should not be able to absorb SA claims.")

issue("4", "No joinder, consolidation or third-party mechanism (co-manufacturers; Ridgeway)", "Critical",
 "SA Art. 14; QA s.7; IPLA s.9; Greenleaf co-manufacturer purchase orders (not reviewed)",
 "None of the three clauses contains any consent to joinder of additional parties, intervention or consolidation with proceedings involving third parties. SA s.15.9 and IPLA s.10.8 exclude third-party beneficiaries.",
 ["Greenleaf's model depends on U.S. co-manufacturers for blending, encapsulation and packaging. The email chain notes that the existing co-manufacturer arrangements use purchase orders with North Carolina choice of law and forum selection for NC state courts, and that a new encapsulation co-manufacturer is expected to come online in Q1 2026.",
  "In a contamination scenario (Mr. Heller's example: a bad curcumin batch processed into 500,000 capsules), Greenleaf will need to blame Pacifica's extraction process and the co-manufacturer's incoming QC at the same time. Under the current documents it would arbitrate against Pacifica (ICC, Singapore seat, London hearings, or SIAC) while suing the co-manufacturer in Mecklenburg County Superior Court. Each respondent would argue the other caused the loss. Greenleaf could lose in both forums on inconsistent findings (\"empty chair\" risk).",
  "Under ICC Rules Art. 7, an additional party can be joined only if it is bound by an arbitration agreement, or (after the tribunal is constituted) if all parties, including the additional party, agree (Art. 7(5)). The co-manufacturers have no arbitration agreement with Pacifica and no incentive to consent. The QA expert determination binds only Greenleaf and Pacifica, so its findings would not bind a co-manufacturer.",
  "Ridgeway (about 62% equity holder; an \"Affiliate\" of Greenleaf under the IPLA definition) has no mechanism to participate. Mr. Park describes this as a secondary concern. We agree: Ridgeway's interests are better protected through confidentiality carve-outs (Issue 15) and governance arrangements with Greenleaf than through a right to intervene."],
 "This is client priority 2 and goes to the core of Greenleaf's most likely loss scenario. Parallel proceedings duplicate cost and evidence-gathering. They also expose Greenleaf to findings in one forum that defeat its claim in the other.",
 ["**Consent to joinder and consolidation.** Pacifica consents, in advance, to the joinder of any Affiliate of either party and of any \"Related Party\" (Greenleaf's co-manufacturers, contract packagers, contract laboratories and carriers) that agrees in writing to be bound. It also consents to consolidation of an arbitration under the Transaction Documents with any arbitration between Greenleaf and a Related Party under a compatible ICC clause, before a single tribunal.",
  "**Greenleaf litigation option for multi-party quality disputes.** Where a claim by Greenleaf against Pacifica arises from the same facts as a claim against a Related Party that is not bound to arbitrate, Greenleaf may elect (within 30 days of the Request for Arbitration or Answer) to have that dispute decided in the state or federal courts sitting in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina (or New York County, New York), and Pacifica submits to that jurisdiction and appoints a U.S. process agent. Singapore and New York courts generally uphold asymmetric option clauses between commercial parties (e.g., Dyna-Jet Pte Ltd v Wilson Taylor Asia Pacific Pte Ltd [2017] SGCA 32), but the clause must be drafted precisely.",
  "**Evidence-sharing covenant.** Pacifica agrees to provide documents, retained samples (QA s.2.3) and witness cooperation in any proceeding between Greenleaf and a Related Party concerning Products, subject to confidentiality protections.",
  "**Greenleaf internal action.** Going forward, including for the Q1 2026 encapsulation co-manufacturer, require co-manufacturing agreements to contain an ICC arbitration clause compatible with the unified clause (same rules, seat and language) and an express consent to joinder and consolidation with arbitrations under the Pacifica Transaction Documents. Consider amending existing co-manufacturer purchase orders on renewal."],
 "If Pacifica refuses the litigation option, insist on (i) the advance joinder/consolidation consent; (ii) a covenant that Pacifica will not object to the tribunal sitting on the same timetable as, or coordinating with, the related court proceeding; and (iii) Pacifica's agreement to be bound by findings of the technical expert (Section VII) that are also put before the court.")
PYEOF
echo ok
EOF
)"
